title_original: You Can See Everything Review: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Extraordinary, Troubling Documentary Evokes the Spirit of Kiarostami

blocks.text: “What requires attention in cinema are the traces of these palpable things ingrained on the cinematic surface.” — Shiguéhiko Hasumi, Directed by Yasujirō Ozu “That everyone in the world, including myself, is totally nuts.” — Nathan Fielder in a 2014 Reddit AMA responding to the question “Nathan, what has your show taught you about human nature?”

Let’s agree Lev Kuleshov was wise to stress a performer’s expression. If Samuel Fuller was also correct for stating, vis-à-vis Jean-Luc Godard, that the love, hate, violence, action, and death strewn across cinema’s battleground all lead towards emotion, we can Frankenstein these two notions into the concept, monstrous or otherwise, that great directors winnow both intellectual and instinctual fascinations to the human face. Ozu found much of lived experience within the pained half-smile; Kubrick externalized id through the head-down, eyes-up glare; “Lynchian,” seemingly indefinable, is often defined by fear in the eyes; Spielberg asks that the eyes (and mouth) go wide to convey awe; Buster Keaton wore a stone expression that only the scariest stunts a filmmaker has ever put themselves through would break, and just into a sort of bafflement.

Nathan Fielder has the uncomprehending stare. The very real people encountered throughout Nathan for You and The Rehearsal tend to look at him—or “Nathan Fielder,” a composite between auteur and selfsame character—half-blank, half-concerned. Sometimes it’s contempt only quelled for the sake of a camera; at other turns it’s an uneasy facsimile of politeness towards this strange man who’s placing an impossible scenario before them; and often their sole recourse is a low-power autopilot. You can find this a hilarious, incisive vision of human behavior or wholly unpleasant showcase for its creator’s misanthropy—these are such questions prodded by artists of serious intent.

Nathan Fielder now wears the uncomprehending stare. He’s directing it at Elizabeth Holmes in the days before her 11-year imprisonment over a nine-figure defrauding for her blood-testing project Theranos, a scam orchestrated at such uncommon size that it must be made into the harshest example. Why she and her husband have trusted Fielder, a constant chronicler of errant human behavior, to craft a sympathetic portrayal of her ostensible plight is never quite clear. Holmes, resembling a Chuck Jones cartoon and sounding like she’s just overcome airway constriction, returns a stare that’s not so much uncomprehending as it is incomprehensible , a vague visage that creates one of this film’s organizing principles: not just for the basic film-grammar question of when to cut between hers and Fielder’s, but how this face, even once cut from, seems to echo and radiate across the scene.

I was thinking about the ping-ponging point-counterpoint between people’s faces—Fielder and Holmes and her husband and some others who show up—through many of the 174 minutes comprising You Can See Everything , his often-extraordinary feature-filmmaking debut during which nearly every expression that can be made with a person’s eyes will occur and recur to our amusement, if not knowledge. A camera has seldom fixated so hard on expressions to crack what is (or might be) resting beneath the surface. It stares and stares and stares : at faces, their musculature, at eyes, their shifts through smiles or frowns, the device like an interrogator forcing a confession or a psychic trying to explode a head. You Can See Everything is vertiginous in its staticity, a concentric circle that expands or contracts by the smallest brush of discomfort; it operates through an inability to manage its own tasks, entering a cocktail-napkin-sized pantheon of films that succeed so brilliantly on the basis of failure.

Though co-directed by Lance Oppenheim—whose involvement Fielder obviously did nothing to discount during a post-screening Q&A, and which one can connect to nothing less than a film du jour —it’s nigh impossible envisioning You Can See Everything as (co-)made by anyone else (or, pending availability, the ghost of Abbas Kiarostami). It is also, by all counts, Fielder’s inaugural time playing straight. This is evident quickly, if not quite instantly: the first laugh earned at a beyond-sold-out New York Film Festival premiere was not from Holmes’ several appearances throughout the opening minute, but from Fielder, and just part of him—an obscured face making what any neophyte would naturally read as a resting expression. It’s a fair-enough response when taken hand-in-hand with the serious-documentary form (slightly overbearing music, greyscale color-grading) this movie wears like an odd suit, and one from which we see the paradox in being a major artist: the deeper one goes to establish their own style, the less a devotee’s willing to let them turn elsewhere.

But it can be hard, once an admirer, to discuss Nathan Fielder without lapsing into overly fawning, even obsequious tones. Yet Nathan for You is replete with Fielder seeming to possess some frightening, Dr. Mabuse-esque capacity for bending reality to his will; it’s no exaggeration to say turning these powers for persuasion and problem-solving towards evil could engender global catastrophe. The authorities exhibited therein haven’t burned quite as bright in the nine years since: The Rehearsal , for whatever honest greatness it has achieved, can suffer in comparison—a tad too strong the sense of controlled experiment, a tad too many seams visible in its editorial practice. You Can See Everything left me considering Fielder’s genius as choosing when or when not to engineer. Acknowledging that this film simply couldn’t have been made in real time or without certain stretches built on careful organization, it’s also his first project since Nathan for You that has the quality and danger of open-air experiment. The camera is not just turned on, we know full well; but once it is and allowed to rest on a subject facing direct, difficult questions, Fielder’s skills for social manipulation thrives on a Rick Rubin-like let-them-be-them philosophy. In a world where everyone, including himself, is totally nuts, Elizabeth Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, just happen to be so on another level. Who inches the other out is a question you may be asking while reading this, then will continue asking after You Can See Everything .

I’ve been less fascinated with Elizabeth Holmes, whom I only knew to identify circa The Dropout , a 2022 miniseries that starred Amanda Seyfried as the turtleneck-wearing, mottle-throated scammer. Clips and contextualizing detail were sufficient; I’ve found it more telling that our culture’s awful habit of eventually affording every cretin actually-they’re-cool plaudits has never been afforded her. I say this to establish a personal bias—likely less than many will bring—that shapes my sense You Can See Everything ’s first stretch lacks much of its own. What these scenes (some built on candid conversation, some a tad more structured) instead exemplify is Fielder’s genius for the open-air investigation—often through his own failure to explain why he’s in Holmes’ seaside house to begin with, and from the contradiction borne of respecting those who have opened their doors but, in so doing, expose habits for which respect is an uneasy match.

Holmes, facing an incredibly harsh future on the basis of her mendacity, stands by the remarkable insistence that she’s never lied. Evans, amidst postures as a nice and caring husband, quickly steps in when his wife can’t whisk eggs fast enough, forcing Fielder to break his interrogation mid-sentence. Holmes claims ignorance towards the notion that words might have more than one direct meaning, leaving her equal parts helpless to explain Theranos’ failure or understand “Who’s on First?” while nevertheless—or for this?—grasping the depth of her situation. Evans downplays the extent of his family’s wealth when Fielder suggests it’s attractive to an erstwhile-billionaire wife. Holmes sends Fielder a text that is both the source for this film’s title and, despite my best efforts to parse, completely incoherent to the conversation they’ve just had or anything I might tether to greater happenings. Evans insists he’s prioritizing spousal care, a performance that spurs disturbing questions amidst his resistance to cooperate during the film’s second half. Or a second half that blooms exclusively through his cooperation and willingness to share (for his sake, for the film’s, for nothing’s) revelation after revelation.

blocks.text: These and many such perplexities abound until we witness Holmes enter prison from behind and afar, vanishing at You Can See Everything near-exact halftime. Whether Fielder and Oppenheim knew where to go next isn’t so obvious. A “Two Years Later” title card launches us from the spring 2023 to late 2025, and subjects now viewing the material we’ve sat through certainly implies thorough editing in that interim. What then ensues deserves discussion and, I’m sorry to say, is highly discouraged from such. The NYFF Q&A began with a notice that it a) should not be recorded by us and b) would not be made public until after the film’s release, a two-factor security system that still found Fielder and Oppenheim cautious to name any person or thing relevant to their movie’s second half.

Suffice to say, Fielder’s career-long investigation-through-recreation method is a more-than-suitable tool for You Can See Everything ’s well-established perspective on duplicity and sycophancy. Nor is it some deep spoiler to note that other figures will, almost by necessity of length, enter the frame. How that front-and-centering alters alchemy is a deeper quandary. Certainly it’s a means for turning inside-out to increasingly uncomfortable degrees, yet at turns I suspected the audience was forming their own obsequious attitude towards new players who, like Holmes, have an inability to articulate what’s directly before them while, unlike the convicted felon, avoiding derisive laughs.

Such ground-shifting choices beget queries about a project so concerned with the way questions can sublimate doubt. Is You Can See Everything ’s somewhat rote soundtrack—notes that get loud and louder until hush , dialogue—and solid but functional palette (often from DP David Bolen’s nevertheless impressive ability to work with a single light source) their play on stock doc form, or a dribbling-out of imagination? Am I talking in circles and making excuses to buttress my intense admiration for this, otherwise a surplus of imagination? Should I not suspect editorial tinkering whenever a conversation “starts” just as the scene begins? How effectively do the recreations parody prestige-TV style without falling into its traps? Am I convinced by its bigger gestures because I want to believe in Fielder’s larger project—which can often seem designed to showcase his genius—thus rendering me a dupe? Why is there not only an image of Evans’ penis, but one that lingers?

I can assert a minimal fascination with Elizabeth Holmes’ inner workings; I can tell you it did nothing to stop my leaning forward during a brief hitch in Nathan Fielder recalling a conversation with her, how this film then hinges on if she once said it or something ; I can voice admiration for his and Oppenheim’s patience to let us ponder that question deep into an extensive runtime as well as I appreciate the sustained reenactment interpolated throughout. You Can See Everything is replete with such tenacity, with a desire to sit as those in frame proceed per their truest selves or wobbly projections, their deficiencies or my own judgements, their charms or a dubious copy. The whole operation suggests being let in on a wild secret told by a person you have no reason to trust. Whether I’m talking about the auteur or subjects is one question; whether the subjects are the auteurs stands to review. This movie could be a dead rabbit pulled from a frayed hat or a benchmark or Fielder and Oppenheim fusing both into something altogether new. I don’t know the answer, I don’t want to tell myself, and I do not trust you to do the same.
You Can See Everything opens in theaters on Friday, October 16.
